    #CA1 S1 (2024 - 2025)

    #Question 1

    Derive an expression for the change in kinetic energy across the engine.

    Change in kinetic energy,

    ΔKE=KEout​−KEin​

    ΔKE=(21​m˙C2)e​−(21​m˙C2)a​

    ΔKE=21​(m˙a​+m˙f​)Ce​2−21​m˙a​Ca​2

    ΔKE=21​m˙a​[(1+f)Ce​2−Ca​2]

    Derive an expression for the thermal efficiency of an engine.
    Define thermal efficiency and discuss its meaning.

    Thermal efficiency,

    ηth​=Q˙​fuel​ΔKE​=m˙f​QR​ΔKE​

    ηth​=m˙f​QR​21​m˙a​[(1+f)Ce​2−Ca​2]​

    ηth​=2fQR​(1+f)Ce​2−Ca​2​

    Assuming f≪1,

    ηth​=2fQR​Ce​2−Ca​2​

    Thermal efficiency is defined as the ratio of the rate of addition of kinetic energy
    to the propellant to the total energy consumption rate.

    It is a measure of the effectiveness of energy conversion from the fuel to potentially useful kinetic energy
    for propulsion.

    #Question 2

    Derive an expression for the overall efficiency of an engine.
    Show that the engine’s overall efficiency     ηo​=2fQR​(Ce​−Ca​)Ca​​.

    From Question 1,

    ηth​=2fQR​Ce​2−Ca​2​ (Assuming f≪1)

    Propulsive efficiency,

    ηp​=ΔKEThrust Power​

    ηp​=21​m˙a​[(1+f)Ce​2−Ca​2]TCa​​

    ηp​=21​m˙a​(Ce​2−Ca​2)m˙a​(Ce​−Ca​)Ca​​ (Assuming no pressure thrust and f≪1)

    ηp​=(Ce​+Ca​)(Ce​−Ca​)2Ca​(Ce​−Ca​)​

    ηp​=Ce​+Ca​2Ca​​

    Overall efficiency,

    ηo​=ηth​×ηp​

    ηo​=2fQR​Ce​2−Ca​2​×Ce​+Ca​2Ca​​

    ηo​=2fQR​(Ce​+Ca​)(Ce​−Ca​)​×Ce​+Ca​2Ca​​

    ηo​=fQR​(Ce​−Ca​)Ca​​

    is not moving in takeoff condition.

    Fan Outlet Properties

    P2​P8​​=rfan​=1.5

    P8​=151.5 kPa

    101P2​​=10.41.4​

    300T8​​=1+0.851​(1.51.40.4​−1)

    T8​=343.35 K

    Fan nozzle

    Critical pressure of nozzle,

    P8​Pcr​​=(1−ηfn​1​γa​+1γa​−1​)γa​−1γa​​

    151.5Pcr​​=(1−2.40.4​)0.41.4​

    Pcr​=80.035 kPa

    Since Pcr​<Pa​, the fan nozzle is unchoked.
    Since it is unchoked, Pef​=Pa​=101 kPa.

    #CA2 S1 (2025 - 2026)

    #Question 1

    Give two limitations of the ramjet engine.

    • Unable to operate at low speeds due to the use of shockwaves to compress air
    • Efficient in the supersonic range (Mach 3~6) but becomes inefficient below M2
    • Cooling challenges due to extreme temperatures at high Mach numbers

    #Question 2

    The propellant in a typical rocket thrust chamber has a pressure Pc​=3.72 MPa and temperature Tc​=2727°C. The propellant flows through the nozzle and exits with a pressure of one atmosphere. Assume the propellant has the same molecular weight
    and specific heat ratio as those of air,     M=28.96 kg/kmol and γ=1.4.
    The universal gas constant is     Ru​=8.314 kJ/kmol⋅K.

    #Part (a)

    If the propellant flowing through the nozzle is isentropic, show that the exhaust velocity can be expressed as a function of the thrust chamber pressure (Pc​), thrust chamber temperature (Tc​), and exhaust pressure (Pe​).

    Ve​=γ−12γRTc​​[1−(Pc​Pe​​)γγ−1​]​

    Assuming zero velocity within the engine, T0,c​=Tc​.

    Stagnation temperature is equal to static temperature.

    Stagnation temperature,

    T0,c​=T0,e​

    Tc​=Te​+2cp​Ve​2​

    Ve​=2cp​(Tc​−Te​)​

    Ve​=2cp​Tc​(1−Tc​Te​​)​

    Ve​=2cp​Tc​[1−(Pc​Pe​​)γγ−1​]​

    Ve​=2(γ−1γR​)Tc​[1−(Pc​Pe​​)γγ−1​]​

    Ve​=γ−12γRTc​​[1−(Pc​Pe​​)γγ−1​]​

    Specific heat,

    γ−1γR​=cp​/cv​−1cp​/cv​​(cp​−cv​)

    γ−1γR​=cp​−cv​cp​​(cp​−cv​)

    γ−1γR​=cp​

    #Part (b)

    Determine the velocity and Mach number at the exhaust nozzle.
    Assume the exhaust pressure is the same as ambient pressure.

    Specific gas constant,

    R=MRu​​=28.968.314​=0.287 kJ/kg⋅K

    Exhaust velocity,

    Ve​=γ−12γRTc​​[1−(Pc​Pe​​)γγ−1​]​

    Ve​=0.42(1.4)(287)(3000)​[1−3720100​1.40.4​]​

    Ve​=1970.3 m/s

    Exhaust temperature,

    Ve​=2cp​(Tc​−Te​)​

    1970.3=2(1005)(3000−Te​)​

    Te​=1068.5 K

    Exhaust Mach number,

    Me​=γRTe​​Ve​​

    Me​=1.4(287)(1068.5)​1970.3​

    Me​=3

    #Part (c)

    The nozzle exit diameter is given as 0.6m.
    Calculate the mass flow rate and thrust.
    Calculate the specific impulse     Isp​.

    Isp​=m˙p​gF​

    Exhaust density,

    Pe​=ρe​RTe​

    ρe​=287(1068.5)1×105​

    ρe​=0.32609 kg/m3

    Mass flow rate,

    m˙p​=ρe​Ae​Ve​

    m˙p​=0.32609π(0.3)2(1970.3)

    m˙p​=181.66 kg/s

    Rocket thrust,

    T=m˙p​Ve​+(Pe​−Pa​)Ae​

    T=181.66(1970.3)+0

    T=357.93 kN

    Note that Pe​=Pa​.

    Specific impulse,

    Isp​=181.66(9.81)357.93×103​=200.85 s

    #EST S1 (2021 - 2022)

    #Question 1

    #Part (a)

    Thrust equation,

    T=(m˙a​+m˙f​)Ue​−m˙a​Ua​+(Pe​−Pa​)Ae​

    Assuming f≪1 and perfectly expanded nozzle,

    T=m˙a​(Ue​−Ua​)

    T=ρa​Ae​Ua​(Ue​−Ua​)

    Exhaust velocity,

    Ue​=2cp​(T5​−Te​)​

    where T5​ is static temperature at nozzle inlet,
    and     Te​ is static temperature at nozzle outlet

    Increasing thrust generation:

    • Increasing exhaust velocity Ue​ increases thrust generation (turbojet)
    • Increasing engine inlet area Ae​ increases thrust generation (turbofan)

    Increasing exhaust velocity:

    • Increasing temperature at which combustion gases enter the nozzle
    • Achieved by increasing the combustion temperature via more fuel
    • Higher fuel consumption is however not desirable
    • More economical to increase engine inlet area

    Fuel consumption parameters:

    • Specific thrust — thrust generated per unit mass of air (higher is better)
    • TSFC — Fuel consumed per unit of thrust generated (lower is better)

    Engine efficiencies:

    • ηth​ — measure of acceleration of fluid per unit mass of fuel consumed
    • ηp​ — measure of thrust generated from the acceleration of fluid

    #Part (b)

    Parameters that impact environment:

    • Thermal efficiency ηth​ (higher is better)
    • Propulsive efficiency ηp​ (higher is better)
    • Specific thrust Ts​ (higher is better)
    • Thrust specific fuel consumption (lower is better)

    The above parameters contain the term m˙f​.

    Required overall efficiency,

    TSFC=Tm˙f​​=ηo​qHV​Ua​​

    1000×360064​=ηo​(45×106)240​

    ηo​=0.3

    Required thrust,

    TSFC=Tm˙f​​=ηo​qHV​Ua​​

    1000×360064​=Tm˙f​​

    T=56250m˙f​

    Required specific thrust,

    Ts​=m˙a​T​

    Ts​=m˙a​56250m˙f​​

    Ts​=56250(0.02)

    Ts​=1125 kg/sN​

    #EST S1 (2022 - 2023)

    #Question 1

    #Part (a)

    Turbojet vs turbofan:

    • Turbofan has an additional fan located before the compressor
    • A large proportion of air that enters a turbofan flows through the bypass duct
    • All of the air that enters a turbojet flows through the engine core
    • Turbojet accelerates a small mass of air to extremely high velocities
    • Turbofan accelerates a large mass of air to lower velocities

    Thrust specific fuel consumption:

    • Turbofan has better TSFC than turbojet
    • Accelerates flow to relatively lower velocities
    • Less fuel required to increase temperature, and thus exhaust velocity
    • Fan increases the mass flow rate, offsets the lower exhaust velocities
    • Large % of thrust is generated by accelerating the bypass air

    #Part (b)

    Commercial aviation (passenger aircraft):

    • Use of sustainable fuels to replace the typical kerosene fuel
    • Biofuels are derived from renewable or waste sources
    • Biofuels have lower emissions compared to kerosene
    • Does not require major modification to current aircraft

    Hydrogen-powered aircraft:

    • Use of hydrogen fuel in smaller aircraft
    • Combustion of fuel creates only water (no emissions)
    • Use of hydrogen fuel cells that convert hydrogen into electricity
    • Propulsion is achieved by electric motors that run on electricity

    #Question 1

    #Part (a)

    Control system:

    • Also known as a closed system
    • A collection of matter of fixed identity
    • Enclosed by an invisible, massless, flexible surface
    • Boundary of system may change position, size and shape
    • Matter cannot pass through the boundary of the system

    Control volume:

    • Also known as an open system
    • Enclosed by an invisible, massless, rigid surface (control surface)
    • Boundary is of constant shape and size that is fixed in space
    • Matter can pass through the boundary of the system

    Preference for control volume approach:

    • If the fluid (air) is treated as a control system, its properties are to be
      analyzed as the fluid flows through the various devices in the engine
    • Changes within the system’s boundary can occur as the fluid flows
    • Difficult to analyze properties if system is constantly changing
    • In the control volume approach, its properties are analyzed at that
      point in the control volume; “window” for observation of the flow
    • Changes in properties can be deduced through energy balance
    • Does not require “following” the same mass of fluid as it flows

    #Part (b)

    External forces acting on control volume:

    • Ambient pressure
    • Thrust of the engine
    • Reaction of the engine support

    #Part (c)

    Unused kinetic energy is energy that is dumped out of the system.
    This energy is wasted as it does not contribute to thrust generation.

    ΔKE across Engine=Thrust Power−Unused KE

    21​m˙a​(Ue​2−Ua​2)=m˙a​(Ue​−Ua​)Ue​−Unused KE

    Unused KE=(m˙a​Ue​2−m˙a​Ua​Ue​)−21​(m˙a​Ue​2−m˙a​Ua​2)

    Unused KE=21​m˙a​Ue​2−m˙a​Ua​Ue​+21​m˙a​Ua​2

    Unused KE=21​m˙a​(Ue​2−2Ua​Ue​+Ua​2)

    Unused KE=21​m˙a​(Ue​−Ua​)2

    Note the underlying assumptions that f≪1 and pressure thrust is negligible.

    #Question 3

    #Part (a)

    Energy balance,

    E˙in​=E˙out​

    E˙a​+E˙f​=E˙ex​

    m˙a​ha​+m˙f​qHV​=(m˙a​+m˙f​)he​

    m˙f​qHV​=(m˙a​+m˙f​)he​−m˙a​ha​

    1st law of thermodynamics,

    Q˙​−W˙=H˙out​−H˙in​

    Q˙​f​=(m˙a​+m˙f​)he​−m˙a​ha​

    m˙f​qHV​=(m˙a​+m˙f​)he​−m˙a​ha​

    Note that net work of a jet engine is zero as all the turbine work output is used to drive the compressor.

    #Part (b)

    Energy balance,

    m˙f​qHV​=(m˙a​+m˙f​)he​−m˙a​ha​

    fqHV​=(1+f)(cp​Te​+2Ue​2​)−ha​

    fqHV​=(1+f)cp​Te​+(1+f)(2Ue​2​)−ha​

    cp​fqHV​+ha​−(1+f)(Ue​2/2)​=(1+f)Te​ (Let the LHS be denoted as A)

    A=(1+f)Te​

    Te​=1+fA​ (1)

    Total stagnation temperature,

    T0,e​=Te​+2cp​Ue​2​

    Ue​=2cP​(T0,e​−Te​)​

    Ue​=2cp​Te​(Te​T0,e​​−1)​

    Ue​=Te​​2cp​(Te​T0,e​​−1)​

    Thrust equation,

    F=(m˙a​+m˙f​)Ue​−m˙a​Ua​

    m˙a​F​=(1+f)Ue​−Ua​

    m˙a​F​=(1+f)Te​​2cp​(Te​T0,e​​−1)​−Ua​

    2cp​(T0,e​/Te​−1)​F/m˙a​+Ua​​=(1+f)Te​​ (Let the LHS be denoted as B)

    B=(1+f)Te​​

    B2=(1+f)2Te​

    B2=(f2+2f+1)Te​

    Te​=f2+2f+1B2​ (2)

    Equating (1) and (2),

    1+fA​=f2+2f+1B2​

    B2+B2f=Af2+2Af+A

    0=Af2+(2A+B2)f+(A+B2)

    0=f2+A2A+B2​f+A2A+B2​

    #Part (b)

    #EST S1 (2024 - 2025)

    #Question 1

    #Part (a)

    When referring to a multi-stage compressor, what is the velocity profile in
    the stator and rotor? Draw a diagram and provide explanation supported
    with relevant concepts.

    • Rotor imparts energy into the flow, causing pressure and flow velocity to increase
    • Stator deflects the flow and converts the additional velocity into static pressure
    • Since total pressure across the stator is constant, increase in static pressure
      results in a decrease in flow velocity

    #Part (b)

    When referring to a single stage of a compressor (rotor-stator), sketch in
    a T-s diagram, the stagnation temperatures for the rotor inlet and outlet,
    and the stator inlet and outlet. Provide an explanation for the diagram
    supported with relevant concepts.

    • Rotor imparts energy into the flow, causing pressure and flow velocity to increase, and thus, total temperature increases since T0​=T+2cp​U2​
    • Stator only deflects the flow to convert the additional velocity into static pressure, total temperature remains unchanged across stator

    #Part (c)

    In a converging nozzle, why is the choking condition achieved at the exit area first? Provide an explanation supported with the relevant concepts.

    • Converging area — inlet area is larger than exit area
    • Exhaust gases enter the nozzle at speeds lower than the speed of sound
    • Since m˙=ρAU, as nozzle area A decreases, flow velocity U increases
    • With sufficient decrease in A, flow velocity reaches M=1 at the exit area
    • Choking occurs as any changes in ambient pressure at the exit area does not increase/decrease m˙ due to a difference in pressures at the inlet and exit area

    #Part (d)

    Explain why the TSFC of a turbofan engine is lower than that of a turbojet engine.

    • Significant portion of thrust of a turbofan is generated by the large fan
    • Turbofan accelerates a larger mass of air to relatively lower velocities
    • Lower combustion temperatures required to achieve lower velocities
    • Less fuel is burned to achieve the required combustion temperatures
    • Turbojet has to accelerate flow to significantly higher velocities

    #Part (e)

    Environmental concerns have increasingly become important considerations
    in aviation. Discuss the key engine performance parameters that can impact
    the environment.

    Parameters that impact environment:

    • Thermal efficiency ηth​ (higher is better)
    • Propulsive efficiency ηp​ (higher is better)
    • Specific thrust Ts​ (higher is better)
    • Thrust specific fuel consumption (lower is better)

    Also, it is discussed in the lecture that propulsive efficiency can be increased
    by decreasing the engine exhaust velocity. What other possible alternative
    would lead to a very large increase in propulsive efficiency?

    Propulsive efficiency,

    ηp​=21​m˙∞​[(1+f)Ue​2−U∞​2]TU∞​​

    To increase propulsive efficiency:

    • Decreasing the mass flow rate m˙∞​
    • Decreasing fuel consumption

    #Part (a)

    Energy balance equations,

    h0,∞​=h0,1​ (inlet)

    W˙comp​=m˙∞​(h0,2​−h0,1​) (compressor)

    αm˙f​qHV​=(m˙∞​+αm˙f​)h0,3​−m˙∞​h0,2​ (burner)

    −W˙turb​=(m˙∞​+αm˙f​)(h0,4​−h0,3​) (turbine)

    (1−α)m˙f​qHV​=(m˙∞​+m˙f​)h0,5​−(m˙∞​+αm˙f​)h0,4​ (afterburner)

    h0,e​=h0,5​ (nozzle)

    Summing the LHS,

    LHS=W˙comp​+αm˙f​qHV​−W˙turb​+(1−α)m˙f​qHV​

    LHS=αm˙f​qHV​+(m˙f​qHV​−αm˙f​qHV​)

    LHS=m˙f​qHV​

    Note that in an ideal Brayton cycle W˙comp​=W˙turb​.

    Summing the RHS,

    RHS=m˙∞​(h0,2​−h0,∞​)              +(m˙∞​+αm˙f​)h0,3​−m˙∞​h0,2​              +(m˙∞​+αm˙f​)(h0,4​−h0,3​)              +(m˙∞​+m˙f​)h0,e​−(m˙∞​+αm˙f​)h0,4​
